The censuses also fit 1856: age 4 in the 1860 census and age 14 in the 1870 census agree with a February 1856 birth and not with February 1857, so 1856 has the stone, the 1900 census and both earlier censuses behind it, and 1857 only the death certificate, whose informant did not know his parents. Whitfield (born January 1868, Mississippi) and his wife Emma (born November 1874, Arkansas), with younger siblings Willie G., Robbie W. and Fannie I. The month and year match the gravestone, the initials and given name match the memorial leads, and he was later known as Clint. W. F. Whitfield and Emma Whitfield are added to the tree but are not linked as his parents here: the census gives only Clinton, and no record naming his parents directly has been examined. Birthplace Arkansas is from that census; Chapel Hill remains a memorial lead. Oklahoma’s death index (OK2Explore, searched 4 November 2026) lists Oliver C. Whitfield, male, dying on 22 March 1941 in McCurtain County, one day after the gravestone’s 21 March; unresolved, and the gravestone date is kept. It also lists a William F. Whitfield dying on 21 July 1944 in McCurtain County, which agrees with a Find a Grave lead for the W. F. Whitfield of the 1900 census but names no relationship. The 1910 census of McCurtain County lists “Clam O.” Whitfield, 16, as son of William F. and Emma Whitfield, and the 1930 census gives O. C. Whitfield’s father as born in Mississippi and his mother in Arkansas; see “Clinton, Clam O. and Oliver C.”  His 1941 McCurtain Gazette obituary gives his birth at Chapel Hill, Arkansas, his arrival at Golden about 1916, and names his father, W. F. Whitfield, among the survivors; his mother Emma Ward is probable. He died on Saturday, 22 March 1941.

MAT_LEWIS_MERRY.dp: Golden, McCurtain County, Oklahoma (buried Glover Cemetery)
MAT_LEWIS_MERRY.note: The 1899 affidavit names Lewis Merry as Bessie’s husband and Ida May Merry’s father. Ida’s 1993 obituary instead gives her father’s initials as J. L.; the official final-roll index lists Louis Merry, age 30, intermarried, roll 1363, on Choctaw card 5754. No parents are attached. The 24 October 1903 commissioner’s letter is addressed to Lewis Merry but calls the applicant Louis Merry in its body and names wife Bessie and child Ida May, directly supporting Lewis/Louis as spelling variants for the same applicant. The 6 October 1902 original is addressed to J. L. Merry at Glover under Choctaw D 128, matching the 1903 letter’s Glover address and 7-D 128 reference. This supports a probable identification of J. L. with Lewis/Louis, not proof or a full first-name expansion. The 18 January 1908 letter returns Louis and Bessie’s marriage documents; its date is not their marriage date. Gravestone at Glover Cemetery: “J. L. Louis Merry, Apr. 10, 1872 – July 1, 1932. Dear Papa, we miss you.” An undated newspaper marriage-license list names “Joshua L. Merry” of Glover marrying Mrs. Mattie Erwin. Together with the 1899–1908 Commission letters (Lewis/Louis/J. L., all at Glover), these make Joshua Louis probable. The Dawes index records him as an intermarried white citizen, age 30, roll 1363, card 5754. Leads from Find a Grave only: born Sevier County, Arkansas; parents John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor; first postmaster at Glover; later marriages to Mattie Ervin (1908), Nancy Martha Gregg (1912) and Martha E. (1919). The clipping that names a “Mrs. Mattie Erwin” is undated and its paper unknown, so the 1908 date and the spelling Ervin rest on the memorial alone. The only Mattie in the Dawes jackets read for this site (card 507) is Mattie E. Clay, Abner Clay’s wife, whom the Commission’s letters address under the name Clay through March 1904; no record read names an Erwin or ties her to Louis Merry, so whether she is the clipping’s Mattie is left open. Also recorded as Joshua Louis “J. L.” Merry. Grant Foreman’s 1928 and George H. Shirk’s 1948 lists from Post Office Department records name Joshua L. Merry as first postmaster at Glover, appointed 26 June 1901, and the Official Registers of 1903, 1905 and 1907 list Joshua L. Merry as Glover’s postmaster; by 1911 the office had another postmaster. The identification of this postmaster with Lewis/Louis of card 5754 is probable. Elma Severn’s 1997 family sketch gives his birth as 10 April 1872 and his death on 1 July 1932 at Golden. Card 5754 itself (examined November 2026) names his parents as Calvin Merry and Elizabeth Merry, both dead and both non-citizens; they are not added to the tree here. The card and the Commission’s 1905 decision place him on the 1896 Choctaw roll as Lewis Merry, Eagle County, number 14822. His enrollment file shows the Commission writing to “J. L. Merry, Glover” on 27 March 1902 about the application of “yourself and your wife, Bessie Merry and your child Ida May Merry,” within the same case (Choctaw D 128) as the Louis Merry hearings, which ties the initials J. L. to Louis directly. He married Bessie Durant on 7 September 1896 at Lukfata; Rev. J. H. Sleeper officiated. His enrollment as an intermarried citizen was granted on 10 January 1905 and approved by the Secretary of the Interior on 14 March 1905. The U.S. Postal Service’s postmaster list for Golden names Joshua L. Merry as postmaster there from 29 February 1916 (Cicero M. Medcalf appointed 30 August 1920), as acting postmaster from 16 January 1922 and as postmaster from 25 March 1924 until Mrs. Dosha L. Shane was named acting postmaster on 2 April 1928. The identification of this Joshua L. Merry with the Lewis/Louis Merry of card 5754 is probable, on the shared full name and place. No Joshua L., Lewis or Louis Merry appears in Oklahoma’s death index for 1932 (searched 4 November 2026, with five years’ variance); the gravestone’s 1 July 1932 therefore has no state record behind it here, which may only reflect an indexing gap. He died at Golden on 1 July 1932, aged 60, after thirteen weeks' illness; his four surviving brothers were Rev. W. R. Merry of Garvin, G. G. Merry of Valliant, F. L. Merry of Orange, California, and B. F. Merry of Canadian, Texas; his daughter Ida was Mrs. Clint Whitfield (McCurtain Gazette, 6 July 1932).

MAT_BESSIE_DURANT.bp: Choctaw County, Indian Territory (as given in a 1997 family sketch)
MAT_BESSIE_DURANT.dp: Golden, McCurtain County, Oklahoma (buried Denison Cemetery, Idabel)
MAT_BESSIE_DURANT.note: In her 1899 affidavit Bessie Merry, age 19, names herself as Ida May Merry’s mother. Ida’s February 1993 Bishinik obituary explicitly names her mother Bessie Durant Merry, strengthening that identity beyond the 2008 descendant notice. The official final-roll index lists Bessie Merry, age 21, roll 15526, on Choctaw card 5754. The 1903 commissioner’s letter names her as Louis Merry’s wife and Ida May’s mother. The Dawes final-roll index lists Bessie Merry, 21, 3/4 Choctaw by blood, roll 15526, card 5754. Her 1899 affidavit gives age 19, which fits a gravestone at Denison Cemetery, Idabel: “Bessie E. Kernell, Nov. 11, 1879 – Mar. 22, 1950.” Find a Grave links that stone to Ida May Merry Whitfield and gives a 1907 marriage to John Frank Kernell. The identification is probable. A 1997 sketch submitted by her granddaughter Elma M. Severn to Life and Times of the Choctaw Original Enrollees gives her birth as 11 November 1878 in “Choctaw County, Indian Territory” (a county name used only from 1907) and her death on 22 March 1950 at Golden; the birth year conflicts with the 1879 on her gravestone. It names no parents. Her own Dawes census card, Choctaw 5754 (examined November 2026 in the National Archives Catalog), names her parents as Peter Durant and Ellen Durant, both dead by the April 1899 application and both of Bok Tuklo County, and says she was on the 1896 Choctaw roll as “Betsy” (Eagle County, number 8644). Card 655 gives the same parents for Ben Durant, probably her brother, and the 1900 testimony of John M. Hodges makes Peter Durant a son of Wilsey Clay. She married Louis Merry on 7 September 1896 at Lukfata, Choctaw Nation, according to the marriage certificate and the Commission’s 1905 decision in his enrollment file. Birth year: the 1997 sketch’s 1878 conflicts with the 1879 on the gravestone, but her age of 19 on card 5754 (26 April 1899) and in her affidavit of 27 April 1899 fits 1879 and would be a year low for 1878, so 1879 is used; this is preferred, not proven. Blood: card 5754, card 655 (for her brother Ben) and the final-roll index give three-quarters Choctaw, while Louis Merry called her a “full blood Choctaw” in his November 1902 testimony; the Commission’s three-quarters is the recorded figure and his phrase is taken as a loose description. Her husband at death is probably John Frank Kernell, born 9 March 1883 in Tennessee, who registered for the draft in April 1942 at Wright City with a Glover mailing address and was counted as a widower of 67 in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, on 11 April 1950; see his record. The marriage itself is not documented. Oklahoma’s death index lists Bessie E. Kernell, female, dying on 22 March 1950 in McCurtain County, the date on her gravestone and in the 1997 sketch for Bessie Merry.

MAT_TYRO_BOX.note: The 1930 census records Violet as his daughter. A family-transcribed obituary names her father as T. S. Box; the identification of Tyro with T. S. is probable. The 1900 census names Alonzo and Emma as parents of a Tyro Box born in May 1888, Texas. A 1917 draft registration for Tyro Stevens Box also gives May 1888 and Texas and places him in McCurtain County. The 1930 census gives his birthplace as Oklahoma, so the match remains probable. His 1967 McCurtain Gazette obituary (transcribed on Find a Grave) gives his birth as 22 May 1888 at Pittsburg, Texas, and sixty years' residence in McCurtain County. It describes him as a retired engineer and Valliant Mason and names his brother Arch Box and sister Mrs. Byrd James. Violet’s 1962 obituary names her father T. S. Box of Millerton, which confirms the T. S. identification. The draft card has Tyro Stevens; the obituary has Tyro Stephen. Parent link to Alonzo and Emma stays probable (1900 census plus matching birth month and year). Also recorded as Tyro Stephen Box. His own April 1942 draft registration at Millerton gives 22 May 1888 and Rockwall County, Texas, a third birthplace beside the obituary’s Pittsburg and the 1930 census’s Oklahoma; it names Mrs. T. S. Box as his contact and is signed Tyro S. Box. The 1950 census lists Tyro S. Box, 61, and Annie F., 63, both born in Texas, in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Siblings found in the 1900 household: Walter, Claudy J. (Claude Joel), Flossie B. (Birdie) and Archie W. Oklahoma’s death index lists Tyro S. Box, male, dying on 5 October 1967 in Choctaw County, where Hugo stands.

MAT_ANNIE_BOX.note: The 1930 census identifies Annie as Violet’s mother. The census does not give her maiden name. Her McCurtain Gazette obituary (30 December 1959, transcribed on Find a Grave) names her daughter Mrs. Louis Whitfield of Golden, her brothers Rob and Walter Logan and her sister Mrs. Bell Culpepper, and says she came from Mount Pleasant in 1906. The Wheelock Cemetery card file at the Broken Bow library names her parents as Dudley Logan and Annie Wedgeworth Logan. Sister Belle Logan Culpepper’s memorial gives the same parents. The parent link is probable; no birth or marriage record naming them has been examined. Her stone appears to read 1958; the newspaper’s 1959 is adopted. Also recorded as Annie F. Logan Box. Oklahoma’s death index lists Annie F. Box, female, dying on 28 December 1959 in Choctaw County, the date of her newspaper notice and the county of the Hugo hospital named there.

MAT_ALONZO_BOX.note: The 1900 census identifies him as father of Tyro Box, age twelve. The identification with the later Tyro in McCurtain County is probable. A family note on Tyro’s Find a Grave memorial also calls Tyro “son of Alonzo & Emillie (Wilkerson) Box.” The original 1900 schedule (Justice Precinct No. 6, Van Zandt County, ED 134, sheet 4B, examined 3 Nov 2026) gives his birth as December 1850 in Arkansas, his father’s birthplace as Alabama and his mother’s as Mississippi, and 23 years of marriage. He was a farmer who owned his farm, with a mortgage. Children at home: Walter, Tyro, Claudy J., Flossie B. and Archie W. No 1880 Soundex card for an Alonzo Box was found for Texas or Arkansas. The Mississippi marriage index gives “A. F. Box,” and the Texas death index is said to list an Alonzo as “Bud Box”; neither has been matched to him with a record that names his parents.

MAT_EMMA_BOX.note: The 1900 census identifies Emma as mother of Tyro Box. A collaborative tree and a family note on Tyro’s Find a Grave memorial (“Emillie (Wilkerson)”) both suggest Wilkerson as her maiden name; an independent original record is still needed. The original 1900 schedule gives her birth as July 1860 in Mississippi, her father’s birthplace as Virginia and her mother’s as Mississippi, 23 years of marriage, and eight children born, six living. It gives no maiden name. No record naming her as a Wilkerson was found in this round. Two Texas birth entries (Claude Joel Box, 1891, and Flossie Bell Box, 1894, both at Rockwall) name the mother as Emily Wilkerson, and two Mississippi marriage entries join an A. F. Box and an Emily Wilkerson in Benton County in 1876 and 1877; see “Emma Box and Emily Wilkerson.” Her maiden name is probably Wilkerson, with Emily as the fuller form.

MAT_CARYLON_LIVESAY_BARDWELL.note: The Pearland Historical Society’s July 2014 newsletter, p. 3, reports her death on 18 June in Carthage and names her parents as Lester and Barbara Livesay, brother Wayne Livesay and late husband Jimmy Bardwell. The identification with this family is probable; no birth date is supplied. The Pearland Historical Society’s April 2024 and January 2025 newsletters list a Carolyn Livesay in the Pearland High School class of 1955 and in a varsity volleyball photograph; probably the same person, whose first name is spelled Carolyn and Carylon in different records. Probably the Carolyn Livesay pictured in the seventh grade in the 1950 Pearland school yearbook.

MAT_CATHERINE_OUIDA_WHITFIELD_CARROLL.note: Her May 2007 Bishinik obituary names her parents Oliver Clinton and Ida May Merry Whitfield and deceased brothers Omagene Clinton and Oliver Lewis Whitfield. She served 22 years at the Golden post office and retired as postmaster in 1990. The father and brother are probable identifications with the existing census-linked people; recorded name-order variants remain visible. The Postal Service’s postmaster list for Golden names Mrs. Catherine O. Carroll acting postmaster on 30 June 1968 and postmaster from 8 January 1969; the next entry, an officer-in-charge, is dated 28 November 1990. That matches the 22 years and the 1990 retirement in her obituary. Oklahoma’s death index lists Catherine Ouida Carroll, female, dying on 16 March 2007 in McCurtain County, matching her obituary. Oklahoma’s birth index lists her as Cathrine Oudla Whitfield, female, born 15 January 1924 in McCurtain County, matching her obituary’s date; the index’s spelling of her middle name is a clerk’s reading of Ouida.

MAT_HATTIE_MYERS_KILGORE.note: Probable identification of William Nelson’s 1920 stepdaughter Hattie Myres with Hattie Myers Kilgore, whose memorial notice names her mother Mrs. Stevens and sister Audrey Nelson. The original certificate for Mrs. Gordon Kilgor records age 20 and 1909 birth year, with day/month and parent information unobtainable. The memorial instead gives 23 September 1906; unresolved. Her father remains unknown.

MAT_NONA_MYERS_ALFORD.note: The original Broken Bow News of 7 March 1940 identifies Nona Alford as Julia Stevens’s daughter and Mrs. L. L. Sandridge’s sister. Identifying the latter as Audrey is strongly supported by her husband, son Larry and family records. The 1919 marriage and daughters’ Social Security entries supply Myers as Nona’s earlier surname. Her father remains unassigned. A proposed later Kinley identity has not been established.

MAT_WESLEY_E_ALFORD.note: The 1919 original marriage names Wesley E. Alford and Nona Myers. Their daughters’ Social Security entries name Wesley, or Wesly, E. Alford as father. A 1940 original Tulsa marriage names the same couple and gives Wesley’s age as 47; identifying it as the earlier pair is probable.

MAT_MABEL_ALFORD_CHIDESTER.note: Social Security NUMIDENT indexes Mabel Alford Chidester, with a later Crowl alias, and names Nona A. Myers and Wesly E. Alford as her parents. The 1940 Camden census names her as Edwin Chidester’s wife. She is the strong match for the unnamed Mrs. Edwin Chidester in the March 1940 family visit. Her 1938 marriage records age 20, conflicting with the 1920 birth date, which would make her 18.

MAT_GERALDINE_ALFORD_FORKNER.note: Her Social Security NUMIDENT entry names Nona A. Myers and Wesley E. Alford as parents and supplies the Forkner alias. A 1992 obituary index identifies Mabel A. Crowl as her sister; the original obituary has not been examined.

MAT_CARL_C_PHILLIPS.dp: Veterans Administration Hospital, Houston, Harris County, Texas
MAT_CARL_C_PHILLIPS.note: Named as Barbara Phillips Livesay’s father in her 1995 obituary. His draft registration (Nacogdoches County) gives Carl Cherry Phillips, born 17 December 1895 in Mississippi; the 1920 census shows him with a wife and daughter Barbara in Montgomery County, Texas; and a 1935 Houston death record for a son names C. C. Phillips and Beulah Turner as parents. His Texas death certificate gives death on 28 April 1960 at Houston and parents John Phillips and Blanche. Those parents are not linked as people. His 1960 death certificate gives his death at the Veterans Administration Hospital, Houston, on 28 April 1960, after 36 years in Houston; a World War I veteran; informant his wife Beulah; buried at Woodlawn Garden of Memories. His mother's maiden name appears only as Blanche.

MAT_BEULAH_TURNER_PHILLIPS.note: Named as Barbara Phillips Livesay’s mother, “Beulah Turner Phillips,” in her 1995 obituary. Her own Social Security application (November 1942) gives birth on 5 February 1900 at Nacogdoches and parents Tom N. Turner and Emory A. Stacy; she is the daughter in the Turner households of 1900 and 1910 at Nacogdoches. The Social Security death index and Texas death index give her death at Houston on 26 February 1993.

MAT_DUDLEY_LOGAN.note: Named as Annie F. Box’s father in the Wheelock Cemetery card file (via her Find a Grave memorial). Her 1959 obituary’s Logan siblings match his children on Find a Grave. Buried Masonic Cemetery, Mount Pleasant, Texas. His memorial says he came to Titus County from Greene County, Alabama; the parents it names are James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun. In 1850 a Dudley, 3, lived in Greene County with Clement Logan, 33, and Mary A., 28, who are linked here as his probable father and possible mother. A widow’s Confederate pension application, number 30414, by Mrs. A. E. Logan of Titus County names her husband as Dudley Logan in the Texas State Library index (index only), implying a claim of Confederate service that no examined record yet details. Leads only: the 1850 census of Greene County, Alabama (USGenWeb transcription), lists a Dudley Logan, aged 3, in the household of Clement Logan, 33, born in South Carolina, and Mary A. Logan, 28; the census does not state relationships, and the mother’s name differs from the Martha Calhoun of his memorial. A Dudley Logan took the voter registration oath in Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, Precinct 24, in 1877. Neither record is proved to be him. The Alabama Department of Archives and History’s Civil War service database has no Dudley Logan (searched November 2026). Update (4 Nov 2026): the 1960 Greene County, Alabama records list a James C. Logan, 1773 to 1840, in the Wedgeworth Cemetery. He died before Dudley’s birth, so he cannot be the “James Clement Logan” father of the memorial; he could be a grandfather (see the story on that cemetery). Nothing is linked. He married Sarah A. E. Wedgworth in Greene County on 18 April 1866. Their first children were born in Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, in 1867 and 1869, the family was still there in 1880, and they moved to Titus County, Texas, by 1886. Parentage proven: named 'Dudley T. Logan' among the three minor heirs and only surviving children of Clemens Logan at the probate of his will on 9 October 1854; paid his share by the executor in 1866-68. In 1860 he and his sister Martha were living in the household of Wm. R. Pool, wagon maker, Havana Beat No. 1, Greene County. Married Miss Sarah A. E. Wedgworth on 18 April 1866 at Mt. Zion Church (licence 16 April; T. S. Winn officiating). His widow's 1914 pension papers say he left Alabama with Capt. Dave Scarborough's cavalry company and was later transferred to a Missouri infantry brigade under Gen. Cockrell, and that the couple came to Texas in 1883. The 'James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun' of his Find a Grave memorial were his grandparents (the grandfather probable).

MAT_ANNIE_WEDGEWORTH_LOGAN.note: Named as Annie F. Box’s mother (“Annie Wedgeworth Logan”) in the Wheelock Cemetery card file via Find a Grave. Her years (1846–1923) come from Find a Grave family links and have not been checked against her own memorial or an original record. The Texas State Library index to Confederate pension applications lists Mrs. A. E. Logan of Titus County, application 30414, widow of Dudley Logan; probably her. Index only; the file was not examined. Lead only: the 1850 census of Greene County, Alabama (USGenWeb transcription), lists Sarah A. E. Wedgeworth, aged 9, in the household of Stephen Wedgeworth, 41, born in North Carolina, and Nancy M. Wedgeworth, 31, nine dwellings from Clement Logan’s household with a three-year-old Dudley. The initials match her full name, but an age of 9 in 1850 points to a birth about 1841, not 1846, and the census does not state relationships. Not linked. Her marriage to Dudley T. Logan, as Sarah A. E. Wedgworth, on 18 April 1866 in Greene County, Alabama, is on record; her daughter Belle Culpepper's and son Willie Clements Logan's death records name her too. In 1900 she was a widow farming her own land in Titus County, aged 53, born September 1846 in Alabama to a South Carolina-born father and Tennessee-born mother, mother of eleven children with eight living. Probably the Annie E. S. Logan who was postmaster of Tuscaloosa, Texas, in 1901. Her pension application (30414, sworn 30 Nov 1914) gives her birth as 15 September 1846 and her marriage as 18 April 1866 in Greene County; she lived in Titus County from 1883, post office Mount Pleasant. Her marriage record calls her Miss Sarah A. E. Wedgworth. Her September 1846 birth fits Larkin Wedgworth's daughter (Ann E., 4, in 1850; Amanda E. J., 13, in August 1860) and not Stephen Wedgeworth's Sarah A. E. (9 in 1850), but the 1860 given name Amanda does not match, so Larkin stays a probable father, not proven. Larkin Wedgworth, her probable father, is proven a son of James Wedgworth Sr. (d. 1843) by his widow Rachel's 1844 will.

MAT_OMAGENE_WHITFIELD.dp: Normandy, France (missing; Tablets of the Missing, Normandy American Cemetery)
MAT_OMAGENE_WHITFIELD.note: Ida’s 1993 obituary: “Her younger son, Omagene Whitfield, was killed during World War II.” Catherine Carroll’s 2007 obituary names her deceased brother Omagene Clinton Whitfield. Tec 5, 300th Engineer Combat Battalion, service no. 38466149, died 19 June 1944; memorialized on the Tablets of the Missing. Presence aboard LST-523 (mined that day) is probable, not proven. Oklahoma’s birth index lists Omagene C. Whitfield, male, born 1 January 1922, the date in the tree, but under Beaver County in the Panhandle, which does not fit the Golden birthplace; unexplained and possibly an indexing error. A letter he wrote from Camp White, Oregon, signed Omagene C. Whitfield, Co. C, 300th Engineers, to his grandmother Bessie and Frank Kernell survives in the family (shared on Ancestry by RHrhenry15).

Update (4 Nov 2026): the 1894 Portrait and Biographical Record sketch of his son Evan Carter Livesay says Lorenzo Dow was born in Virginia in 1806, left it at twelve with his father John Livesay for Tennessee, moved to Illinois in 1827, settled near Nashville, and later went to Kansas, where he died in 1876. His wife was Delilah Mayse, who died two years before him. The 1806 birth fits the land patent and census better than the veterans’ list estimate of about 1815. The sketch and the veterans’ list agree that his father was named John, so he is now linked to John Livesay as a probable son; Rebecca Carter is named as his mother only by the veterans’ list and is not linked.

xs9-001.note: Named as Bessie Merry’s father on her own Dawes census card, Choctaw 5754, which marks him dead and gives Bok Tuklo as his county; the same card names her mother Ellen Durant. Card 655 names him, dead, of Bok Tuklo, as father of Ben Durant. At the Commission hearing at Atoka on 7 December 1900, John M. Hodges, aged fifty, testified that he knew Peter Durant, that Peter had two small children, a girl and a boy, when Hodges left that part of the country in 1877 or 1878, that Peter was mixed blood (“about a quarteroon”) and his wife Choctaw, and that Peter was the son of Woolsey Clay and a half brother of Abner Clay. The card gives Bessie and Ben three-quarters Choctaw blood, which does not fit Hodges’ estimate exactly. His birth date, birthplace and death date are unknown. A 1920 McCurtain County Court heirship notice for Lizzie McGee names Peter Durant, deceased, as a maternal uncle of Lizzie, whose maternal grandmother was Wilsey Clay: a second record making him Wilsey's son.

xs9-002.note: Named as Bessie Merry’s mother on Dawes census card Choctaw 5754 and as Ben Durant’s mother on card 655, both times marked dead, of Bok Tuklo County. John M. Hodges testified in 1900 that Peter Durant’s wife was Choctaw, “about a half breed” in his estimate, but he did not name her. Her maiden name, parents and dates are unknown.

xs9-003.note: Listed on Dawes census card Choctaw 655, in the household of his grandmother Wilsey Clay at Red River post office, Bok Tuklo County: Ben Durant, grandson, 18, male, three-quarters Choctaw, son of Peter Durant and Ellen Durant, both dead, of Bok Tuklo. The card says he was on the 1896 roll in Blue County and also, as Benj. Durant, in Bok Tuklo County, and that he died on 28 September 1901; proof of death was filed on 25 March 1902 and he was dismissed from the rolls in 1905. Because Bessie Merry’s card 5754 names the same parents with the same county and status, he is probably her full brother. His birth year is estimated from his age at the April 1899 application.

xs9-004.note: Head of Dawes census card Choctaw 655: Wilsey Clay, 58, full blood, Bok Tuklo County, post office Red River, on the 1896 roll as number 2573, Dawes roll 1552; her parents are given as Joe Cahn and Patsey Cahn, both dead, of Eagle County. The card lists her daughter Ida and grandchildren Ben and Licey Durant. Card 507 names her as mother of Abner H. Clay and card 656 as mother of Laura Durant. That she was Peter Durant’s mother, and so Bessie Merry’s grandmother, rests on John M. Hodges’ sworn testimony of 1900 (“Peter Durant was the son of Woolsey Clay”) together with card 655, which makes Peter’s son Ben her grandson; probable. Her maiden surname is inferred only from her parents’ names on the card. Also spelled Woolsey in the 1900 transcript. Her age differs between records: 58 on card 655 (April 1899) gives a birth about 1841, but she gave her age as 67 when sworn at Lukfata on 9 May 1906, which points to about 1839; the tree keeps about 1841 and the difference stays unresolved. In that 1906 testimony, in the Dawes jacket for card 966, she also swore that she was the mother of Thomas Durant, Lizzie Durant Gibbs’s father (proven by her own answer). In the 1920 heirship petition for her granddaughter Lizzie McGee (Choctaw roll 3353, died about February 1906) she is named as maternal grandmother; her children there are Peter Durant, Thomas Durant, Abner Henry Clay and Emma Costilow, all deceased, Laura Dyer, Ida Bunch, and Lizzie's unnamed mother.

The Nashville Masonic lodge list of 1848–49 names him with his stepson George T. Hoke and S. M. Carter. E. 1/4 Sec. 7,” a year after a Methodist minister named Robert Carter settled the next section. That fits the 1879 county history’s statement that Livesay Carter came to Illinois in 1818 and lived about four years in what is now Clinton County. If the cemetery list’s birth of 15 November 1799 is right he was eighteen on that day, young to enter a quarter section in his own name.

xt3-001.note: Named on Dawes census card Choctaw 507 as Mattie Clay, 26, intermarried white (I.W. 699), wife of Abner H. Clay, daughter of Joseph H. Denson and Mattie E. Denson, both non-citizens. The Commission’s decision of 2 March 1904 calls her “Mattie Clay (nee Denson)” and records her marriage to Abner on 20 May 1897. Her stated age varies: 26 in May 1899, 27 in October 1899 and 32 in December 1902, so her birth year is only about 1870 to 1873. After the couple separated in October 1902 she gave her address as Lockesburg, Arkansas. Her later life has not been traced.

xt3-002.bp: Lukfata, Bok Tuklo County, Choctaw Nation
xt3-002.note: Born 29 March 1898 at Lukfata according to his mother’s and the midwife Amanda Butler’s affidavits of 1 May 1899; Choctaw by blood, three-eighths, roll 1027 on card 507, approved 12 December 1902. Later life not traced.

xt3-003.bp: Lukfata, Bok Tuklo County, Choctaw Nation
xt3-003.note: Born 25 September 1899 at Lukfata according to her mother’s affidavit sworn 20 October 1899 before John H. Sleeper, notary public; Choctaw by blood, three-eighths, roll 1028 on card 507, approved 12 December 1902. Later life not traced.

xt3-004.note: Born 8 March 1902 according to her mother’s affidavit (sworn 24 October 1902, post office Shawneetown) and the midwife Jane Butler’s (29 October 1902); Choctaw by blood, three-eighths, roll 14562. Card 507 notes that she was enrolled on 4 November 1902, and the Secretary of the Interior approved her on 20 May 1903. Her parents separated in October 1902, seven months after her birth. Later life not traced.

xt3-005.note: Named once, by Mattie Denson Clay in her sworn testimony of 16 December 1902, as the former wife of Abner H. Clay, “dead four years” at the time of his marriage to Mattie on 20 May 1897, so dead by about 1893. No record of her own has been found; her maiden name, birth and any children are unknown. Entered as probable because the only source is a second-hand statement.

xt3-006.note: Named on Dawes census card Choctaw 507 as father of Mattie Clay, a non-citizen of the Choctaw Nation. A letter of 29 January 1903 in the jacket is addressed to Claude Denson of Shawneetown, Indian Territory, who describes himself as Mattie Clay’s brother, which supports but does not prove the family name. Nothing else about Joseph H. Denson has been found.

xt3-007.note: Named on Dawes census card Choctaw 507 as mother of Mattie Clay, a non-citizen of the Choctaw Nation. Her maiden name is not given and nothing else about her has been found.

xt3-008.dp: Bok Tuklo County, Choctaw Nation (lived at Lukfata)
xt3-008.note: Wilsey Clay swore on 9 May 1906 that she was his mother, that he “died several years ago,” that his wife was Melinda Durant and that he had two daughters, Jane and Lizzie (or Licey). His daughter Lizzie swore on 14 May 1906 that her father was Thomas Durant, who lived at Lukfata in Bok Tuklo County. Card 655 calls Licey “daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant” and lists her as Wilsey Clay’s granddaughter. His birth and death dates and his own father are unknown.

xt3-009.note: Named as Thomas Durant’s wife by Wilsey Clay and as her mother by Lizzie Gibbs in 1906; Lizzie gave Wolfe County as the county of her mother’s tribal enrollment. Card 966 names her as the mother of Lizzie Durant. Her maiden name, dates and parents are unknown.

xt3-010.note: Enrolled as Lizzie Durant on card 966 (roll 2580, full blood, Wheelock Seminary, 27 April 1899) and, by a clerical duplication that she and her grandmother explained under oath in 1906, also as Licey Durant on card 655. Married Fred Gibbs on 31 March 1902 and had a son, Isaam, on 30 August 1902. Her ages vary with the record (13 in 1899, 18 in 1902, 23 in 1906), so she was born about 1883 to 1886. Later life not traced.

xt3-011.note: Named only once, by Wilsey Clay on 9 May 1906, as one of Thomas Durant’s two daughters and living. No card, age or later record for her has been found.

xt3-012.note: Of Lukfata, aged 21 on the marriage license of 24 March 1902, and a citizen of the United States, not of the Choctaw Nation, on his son’s birth affidavit. Husband of Lizzie Durant. His parents and later life are unknown.

xt3-013.note: Born 30 August 1902 to Fred and Lizzie Gibbs, post office Glover, according to the affidavits of his mother and the midwife Susion Franklin, both sworn before J. L. Merry, notary public, on 1 December 1902. Enrolled as an infant citizen by blood (one-half Choctaw, roll 14616) and approved 8 December 1902. The spelling varies (Isaam, Isaan, Isom). Later life not traced.

xt3-014.note: Head of Dawes census card Choctaw 656: William A. Durant, 29 in April 1899 (32 pencilled later), one-half Choctaw, on the 1896 roll in Nashoba County as number 3382, residence Red River, post office Garvin, Dawes roll 1555, approved 12 December 1902. His parents are Allington Durant and Mary Durant, both dead, of Red River. His wife on the card is Laura, Wilsey Clay’s daughter. The three boys on the card have a different mother. No link to Peter or Thomas Durant is shown on any record read.

xt3-015.note: Named as father of William A. Durant on card 656, marked dead and of Red River County. Nothing else about him has been found; the spelling is as written on the card.

xt3-016.note: Named as mother of William A. Durant on card 656, marked dead and of Red River County. Nothing else about her has been found.

xt3-017.note: Named on card 656 as the mother of Gibby, Eddie and Louie Durant, whose father is given as William A. Durant (number 1 on the card); she is marked dead and of Red River County. The card does not call her William’s wife, so the marriage is inferred from the children. She was dead by April 1899. Her maiden name and dates are unknown.

xt3-018.note: Son of William A. Durant and Sarah Durant (dead) on card 656: aged 8 in April 1899, one-half Choctaw, on the 1896 Nashoba County roll as number 3383, approved 12 December 1902. Laura, aged 19 in 1899, cannot be his mother. Later life not traced.

xt3-019.note: Son of William A. Durant and Sarah Durant (dead) on card 656: aged 6 in April 1899, one-half Choctaw, on the 1896 Nashoba County roll as number 3384, approved 12 December 1902. Laura, aged 19 in 1899, cannot be his mother. Later life not traced.

xt3-020.note: Son of William A. Durant and Sarah Durant (dead) on card 656: aged 5 in April 1899, one-half Choctaw, on the 1896 Nashoba County roll as number 3385, approved 12 December 1902. Laura, aged 19 in 1899, cannot be his mother. Later life not traced.

xt4-001.note: Listed in the Masonic Cemetery, Mount Pleasant, Texas, transcription as born 20 April 1876 and died 15 August 1889, “Son of D. & Annie Logan.” The initials D. and Annie fit Dudley Timothy Logan and his wife, and Dudley lies in the same cemetery, so the parent link is probable. It rests on a transcription of the stone, which was not seen. Neither birthplace nor place of death is given.

xt4-002.note: Listed in the Masonic Cemetery, Mount Pleasant, Texas, transcription as born 23 February 1880 and died 15 November 1888, “Son of D. & Annie Logan,” with the compiler’s remark that the monument is broken and unreadable. Probable child of Dudley Timothy Logan and his wife for the same reasons as his brother Ernest. He is known only from that transcription.

xs7-001.dp: Steele’s Creek, west of Prescott, Nevada County, Arkansas
xs7-001.note: Prescott newspapers of May 1909 report that “Mrs. Clint Sandridge” drowned in Steele’s Creek on Monday, 10 May 1909, trying to save five-year-old August Dierks Jr., and was buried at Midway. The Nevada County Picayune calls her a daughter of the late H. C. Bolls and says she left a husband and three children. The notices do not print her given name; identifying her as Esther Margaret Bolls Sandridge rests on the memorial data recorded in earlier research (born about 1883, died 1909, buried at Midway). The birth year is from that memorial and is unconfirmed.

xs7-002.note: Known only from the Nevada County Picayune of 13 May 1909, which says that Mrs. Clint Sandridge was “a daughter of the late lamented H. C. Bolls.” He had therefore died before May 1909. His full name, dates and residence are not known.

xs7-003.dp: Kerr County, Texas (buried Midway Cemetery, Nevada County, Arkansas)
xs7-003.note: Birth year, death date and place come from his government headstone and memorial as recorded in earlier research (Clinton’s story). An Everett, or Everette, Sandridge is on Prescott school honor rolls in 1915 and wrote to Santa Claus in the Prescott Daily News in December 1916; identifying him with Clinton and Esther’s son is probable, since the papers name no parent.

xs7-004.note: Memorials recorded in earlier research name Mildred Marie, born 1908, as the youngest of Clinton and Esther’s three children; the May 1909 Prescott Daily News says one of Mrs. Sandridge’s three children was an infant. A Mildred Sandridge wrote to Santa Claus in the Prescott Daily News in December 1916. Her later life and death are not known. Clinton’s 1961 notice names two surviving daughters, in California and Houston, but not by name.

xs7-005.note: Probably the brother “Lon, of Little Rock” named in Clinton’s 1961 death notice. Prescott papers record Lon Sandridge’s 1908 arrest for wearing government clothes and Lon P. Sandridge’s March 1912 marriage to Willie Denson; Malvern papers list Lon P. Sandridge among Hot Spring County draft registrants in 1917 and Lon, or L. P., Sandridge among Moline Lumber Co. employees with C. L., or Clint, Sandridge in 1918. Memorials read in earlier research give him the years 1889–1974 and the parents William D. and Mary E. Sandridge; that parentage is unconfirmed, so he is not linked to Clinton in the tree.

xs7-006.note: The Prescott Daily News of 27 March 1912 reports her marriage to Lon P. Sandridge on the previous Saturday afternoon at the home of her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Jim Denson. Monroe and J. M. Denson worked at the Moline Lumber Co. in Malvern with the Sandridges in 1918; their relationship to her is not stated.

xs7-007.note: Listed as “Francis E.,” wife of William A. Nelson, in the 1900 census of Lick Creek Township, Little River County, Arkansas: 29, born April 1871 in Mississippi to parents born in South Carolina, married seven years, mother of three children, two living. The middle initial could also be read as C. Her maiden name is not stated; the index card lists a Harriet McLaren, about 70, born in Maryland, as William’s mother-in-law, which conflicts with the South Carolina birthplace given for Francis’s mother. Her later life is unknown.

xs7-008.note: Daughter, 5, in William A. Nelson’s 1900 household in Little River County, Arkansas, born August 1894 in Texas. William’s memorial, read in earlier research, lists a daughter Rosa Isabel Nelson Flowers (1894–1985); the census writes her middle initial as B. Identifying the two is probable but the later Flowers marriage is unconfirmed here.

xs7-009.note: Daughter, 2, in William A. Nelson’s 1900 household in Little River County, Arkansas, born December 1897 in Texas. Nothing later is known about her.

xs7-010.note: Julia’s last husband. The 1950 census of Broken Bow (ED 45-4, sheet 5, line 14) lists Charley M. Ratcliff, 68, widowed, born in Missouri, living alone three dwellings from Julia A. Stevens. Their 19 August 1950 Sevier County, Arkansas, marriage record was examined in earlier research (Julia’s story). His first wife and his death are not established here.

xu2-001.dp: Grand Prairie Township, Jefferson County, Illinois
xu2-001.note: The 1883 History of Jefferson County calls Robert White the father of Mrs. Tabitha Baldridge and says he was a native of South Carolina who came to Madison County, Illinois, in 1810. The 1909 History of Marion County calls him Rev. Robert White, “a minister in the Methodist Episcopal church, having a large circuit,” who lived early in Indiana, came to Marion County, then settled in Grand Prairie Township, Jefferson County, and names his children: Robert, Martha, Louisa and Tabitha. The Gilead Cemetery transcription lists “White, Rev. R.,” died 14 May 1828, “about 55y,” which would put his birth about 1773. That the stone is his rests on the initial, the title and the township. The two sketches disagree about his earlier life (Indiana or Madison County).
kv: Gilead Cemetery: Rev. R. White, d. 14 May 1828, about 55

xu2-002.note: The 1883 History of Jefferson County names Tabitha Baldridge’s mother as Sarah Holt, a native of North Carolina who was “married in Georgia.” The 1850 census of Jefferson County lists a Sarah White, 74, born in North Carolina, in dwelling 445 with Peter and Rachel Dalson, next to Allan Dalson’s household and two dwellings from the Flannigans’; the identification rests on the name, birthplace, age and neighbors, and the census gives no relationships. Only Tabitha is linked to her as a child, because the sketches name no mother for Martha or Louisa.
kv: Jefferson County, dwelling 445: Sarah White, 74, born NC

xu2-003.note: The 1883 History of Jefferson County says Mrs. Tabitha Casey, widow of Isaac Casey and daughter of Robert White, married James C. Baldridge on 8 January 1846 and was born at Chambers’ Fort on 10 July 1811. The 1909 History of Marion County gives the same birth date and her death on 13 April 1899, and the Gilead Cemetery transcription lists Tabitha Baldridge, 10 July 1811 to 13 April 1899. Her sister Martha was the wife of Thomas Flannigan. The 1850 census lists her as Tabitha, 39, born in Illinois, in dwelling 440, with Casey children and Baldridge children in the house. Her first husband Isaac Casey is not added.
kv: Isaac Casey, then James C. Baldridge, 8 Jan 1846

xu2-004.note: The 1883 History of Jefferson County gives his birth in Rutherford County, North Carolina, on 10 December 1811, as a son of Dornton and Mary (Boggs) Baldridge, who came to Jefferson County in November 1820, and his marriages to Margaret Rainey (20 July 1832) and to Mrs. Tabitha Casey (8 January 1846). The 1909 sketch of his son George Pliney gives his death on 16 May 1897, as does the Gilead Cemetery transcription. His first wife Margaret Rainey is not added.
kv: 10 Dec 1811, Rutherford County, North Carolina (1883 sketch)

xu2-005.note: The 1909 sketch of George Pliney Baldridge says Louisa White married Allen Dolson and had a daughter Sarah, and the 1909 sketch of Eli Copple names Sarah’s parents as Allen and Mary Louisa (White) Dolson and says his wife was born in Georgia. The 1850 census lists Mary L. Dalson, 40, born in Georgia, in dwelling 444. Her birth year is from that age. Her mother is not named in the sketches.
kv: Jefferson County, dwelling 444: Mary L. Dalson, 40, born GA

xu2-006.note: The 1909 sketch of Eli Copple says Allen Dolson was a native of New York near Albany, a son of Peter and Rachael (Quinby) Dolson, who went west as a boy, came to Carlyle, Illinois, and then to Grand Prairie in Jefferson County, where he entered government land, and later lived and died in Marion County. The 1850 census lists Allan Dalson, 45, a farmer born in New York, in dwelling 444 with a household of ten, and a Peter Dalson, 75, and Rachel, 73, both born in New York, in dwelling 445. The 1840 census transcription lists Allen Dolson and Peter Dolson on pages 310a and 309a. His birth year is from the 1850 age.
kv: Jefferson County, dwelling 444: Allan Dalson, 45, farmer, born NY

xu2-007.note: The 1894 and 1909 county biographies give his birth in Washington County, Indiana, as a son of David Copple and Lavina Huckleberry, his move to Marion County, Illinois, at twelve, his marriage in 1840 to Martha Flannagan, who died in 1850, and his marriage in February 1851 to Sarah Dolson. The Jefferson County marriage list gives 5 December 1839 for Eli Copple and Martha Flanagan. The Gilead Cemetery transcription lists Eli Copple, 8 June 1820 to 14 August 1905; the 1909 sketch gives 14 August 1905 and a birth date of 8 January 1820, and the 1894 sketch gives 8 June 1820.
kv: Martha Flanagan, 5 Dec 1839; Sarah Dolson, Feb 1851

xu2-008.note: The 1909 sketch of George Pliney Baldridge says Martha White married Thomas Flannigan and had a daughter Martha who became Eli Copple’s wife; the 1909 and 1894 sketches of Eli Copple give his first wife as Martha Flannagan or Flanagan, a native of Jefferson County who died in 1850. The Jefferson County marriage list gives 5 December 1839 for Eli Copple and Martha Flanagan, and the Gilead Cemetery transcription lists “Copple, Martha,” 1 June 1850, “w/o E.” The sketches give no dates for her birth. Whether the Thomas Flannigan of the White sketch is the Thomas A. of the 1850 census and Thos. H. of the stone rests on place, his wife’s name and this daughter.
kv: Gilead Cemetery: Martha Copple, 1 Jun 1850, w/o E.

xu2-009.note: The 1909 sketch of Eli Copple says he married Sarah Dolson, daughter of Allen and Mary Louisa (White) Dolson, in February 1851, and that she was still living in 1909 in Centralia Township; the White sketch calls her the cousin of his first wife. The Gilead Cemetery transcription lists Sarah Copple, 8 December 1829 to 24 October 1915, in the same cemetery as Eli; the identification rests on the name and place. The 1850 census lists Sarah Dalson, 20, born in Illinois, in her father’s household.
kv: Gilead Cemetery: Sarah Copple, 8 Dec 1829 to 24 Oct 1915

xu2-010.note: The 1883 History of Jefferson County says Lorenzo M. Livesay married Sarah S. Lane, daughter of Henry Lane (deceased), on 16 May 1869; that she was born in Caldwell County, Kentucky; and that she came with her parents to Clinton County, Illinois, in 1840. The 1870 census of Webber Township lists Sarah S., 36, born in Kentucky, in his household, which gives her birth year. Her death has not been found.

xu2-011.note: The 1894 sketch of her son Evan Carter Livesay names his parents as Lorenzo Dow and Delilah (Mayse) Livesay and says she died two years before her husband, who died in 1876, in Kansas. The 1855 Washington County state census counts a woman aged 40 to 50 in L. D. Livesay’s household. Her birth and her marriage have not been found.

xu2-012.note: His own 1894 sketch gives his birth near Nashville, Illinois, on 4 March 1830 as the fourth child of Lorenzo Dow and Delilah (Mayse) Livesay, and says he farmed 115 acres on section 24, Ashley Township, Washington County, married in 1849, had nine children (two deceased by 1894) and was a Methodist and a Populist. The sketch is the only source seen for his birth and parents. His death has not been found.

xu2-013.note: The 1894 sketch of Evan Carter Livesay says he married in 1849 Martha D., daughter of John and Sarah (Coten) Carter, who came from South Carolina to Georgia, then Tennessee and Illinois, and that she was a member of the Christian Church. Her parents are not added, and nothing found says how this Carter family related to Livesay Carter. A duplicate record from an imported family tree, now merged into this one, named John Carter and Sarah Coten Carter as her parents. That parentage is not verified and is not shown in the tree.

xu2-014.note: His own sketch in Brinkerhoff’s 1909 History of Marion County gives his birth on 28 September 1845 as the eldest of eight children of W. E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay, his enlistment in Company C, 60th Illinois, in 1864 under Captain Simeon Walker, his marriage to Emma Ingram on 12 June 1871 and his store at 103 South Locust Street, Centralia. The Adjutant General’s roster lists Jackson L. Livesay of Richview, enlisted 20 March 1864, mustered out 31 July 1865. A volunteer abstract of the muster rolls gives his birthplace as Jefferson County, where the sketch says Washington, Illinois. The 1916–1950 Marion County death index lists a Jackson Lafayette Livesay who died at Centralia on 25 August 1930; the match rests on the name and place.

xu2-015.note: The 1909 sketch of her husband Jackson L. Livesay says he married Emma Ingram on 12 June 1871, that she was the daughter of H. P. Ingram and Millie Tyler of Richview and the second of four children, and that they had nine children. Her parents are not added. Her dates have not been found.

xu2-016.note: His own 1909 sketch gives his birth on 10 May 1861 in Washington County, Illinois, as a son of Alfred Livesay and Hannah (Logan) Livesay, and says he was Supervisor of Foster Township, married Mollie Chick of Foster Township in February 1883 (she died in 1895), had five children, farmed in section 29 of Foster Township, and was a Democrat and a Methodist. His death has not been found.

xu2-017.note: The 1909 sketch of J. R. Quayle says he married Lyda E. Livesay, daughter of Alfred and Hannah Livesay of Patoka Township, on 8 January 1889, that they had four children (two had died by 1909), and that she died in June 1906. Both sketches of Alfred and of Harvey call her Liddie or Lydia and her husband Robert Quale; the Quayle sketch gives the initials J. R.

xu2-018.note: Both 1909 sketches of Alfred and Harvey Livesay name him among Alfred’s children; the first says he married Rachael Walton and had nine children, the second that he was a farmer at Foley, Missouri. The Marion County marriage list gives Marshall A. Livesay and Rachel C. Walton twice, on 20 January 1880 and 20 January 1881. The 1909 sketch of Orville T. Walton names his sister Rachel as the wife of Marshall Livesay of Foley, Missouri. His dates have not been found.
kv: Rachel C. Walton, 20 Jan 1880 (register lists 1880 and 1881)

xu2-019.note: Named in both 1909 sketches as a farmer of Patoka Township who married Laura Cruse and had three children. The Marion County marriage list gives Daniel R. Livesay and Laura O. Cruse on 7 August 1889, and the 1916–1950 death index lists a Daniel R. Livesay who died at Centralia on 28 March 1946, with no age; the identification of the second entry rests on the name.

xu2-020.note: Named first among Alfred’s children in both 1909 sketches: a druggist at Stanley, Iowa, who married Eliza Seward and had four children. The Marion County marriage list gives William T. Livesay and Eliza A. Seward on 16 November 1871. His dates have not been found.

xu2-021.note: Both 1909 sketches say she was single and living at home with her mother, Hannah, in Patoka Township. The 1916–1950 Marion County death index lists an Elizabeth R. Livesay who died at Patoka on 16 March 1934, with no age; the match rests on the name and place.

xu2-025.note: The 1909 sketch of Harvey R. Livesay names his maternal grandfather as James R. Logan, born in South Carolina, who lived in Tennessee until he came to Washington County, Illinois, where he had a well improved farm until his death in 1860; he was a Methodist and a local exhorter. The Washington County probate index lists “Logan, Jas. R., Estate.” His wife and his other children are not named in the sketch. Whether he was the father of James L. Logan, who married Unity Jane Livesay in 1849, is a lead only. 1850 census, District 20, Washington County: James R. Logan, 53, farmer, born South Carolina, with Rachael, 48, and Lewis A., Docia H., Daniel S., Darea E., Martha A. C. and Thomas W. J. 1860 census (1 August, T2S R2W, post office Nashville): Jas. R. Logan, 63, real estate $4,000, with Rachel, 58, born Tennessee, Darcus, Martha A. C. and Thos. W. J.; neighbours John P. Logan, 39, born Tennessee, and Daniel L. Logan, 19; Alfred and Hanah Livesay four doors on, with a son Jas. R., 5. He was alive in August 1860.

xu2-022.note: His 1879 sketch in the History of Washington County says he was born in Harrison County, Indiana, on 1 October 1819, a son of John Hoke, a native of Kentucky who died at Baton Rouge in 1821, and of a Moore from Jefferson County, Kentucky, who married Livesay Carter in July 1823. He married Rebecca Fulton on 4 October 1844, kept a store at Nashville and then at Richview, was Justice of the Peace from 1856, a notary and, in 1876, a county commissioner, and was a Republican, a Methodist and a Mason. His death has not been found. His wife and his father are not added.

xu2-023.note: A physician at Patoka, Marion County, in 1881, partner in a drugstore with Dr. J. B. Lewis and co-founder of the Patoka Enterprise, an elder of the Patoka congregation, who married Mrs. Annie M. Watts on 27 October 1886 and was dead by 1909, when his widow Anna M., a daughter of the Patoka merchant W. K. Simcox, is named. The 1909 sketch of Alfred Livesay calls him a cousin of Alfred. Whether he was the Thomas Newton Livesay, born 22 February 1836, whom the family sketch lists among the children of Robert and Lydia Livesay, is a lead only; he is not linked. Died at Patoka on Tuesday, 10 January 1905 (Salem Republican, 12 Jan 1905; St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 11 Jan 1905).
kv: Thomas N. Livesay and Mrs. Annie M. Watts, 27 Oct 1886

xu2-024.note: The 1879 sketch of Dr. William D. Carter says he began to study medicine, about 1858, in the office of his brother, S. M. Carter, of Pinckneyville, Illinois. The 1879 history lists an S. M. Carter among seventeen men raised in Washington Lodge No. 55 at Nashville in its first year under charter, with Livesay Carter and George T. Hoke, and again among its surviving early members; the 1883 history of Perry County lists S. M. Carter among the five trustees elected when Pinckneyville incorporated in March 1857. His given name, dates and wife are not given in these sources. A Samuel M. Carter appears in the 1850 Perry County census listing and an S. M. Carter, with Malissa and four children, in the 1860 listing, but those transcriptions give names only, so they are not tied to him.

xu3-001.note: James Leaton’s 1883 History of Methodism in Illinois gives his birth in Jackson County, Georgia, on 13 April 1802, his conversion at a Shiloh camp-meeting in 1819, his admission to the conference in 1830, six children by 1834, a twenty-two-year location from 1834, his return to circuits in 1856, his service from 1863 as chaplain of the Fifteenth Illinois Cavalry, and his death on 22 February 1880 at his son’s residence at Carbondale. The state roll of the 15th Illinois Cavalry lists a chaplain Simeon Walker from 5 June 1863 to 25 August 1864. The 1879 county history says a Rev. Simeon Walker still lived at Richview in the home of his son. Levi’s 1921 memoir names Simeon as his father. That he is the father of Captain Simeon Walker of Richview is probable, from the 1850 household, the “Jr.” in the 1852 marriage record and the Richview residence; no record opened states it. The 1850 census gives a Kentucky birthplace for the Simeon Walker, 48, of dwelling 280, which conflicts with Leaton’s Georgia. His parents are linked as leads: his son Levi’s notes of about 1905 name them as Abram Walker (d. January 1812, Livingston County, Kentucky) and Rhoda Beauchamp, who married Henry Sharp in 1815. That is one family source, and it differs by a year or two from other accounts of the family’s move.
kv: Chaplain, 15th Illinois Cavalry, 5 Jun 1863 to 25 Aug 1864
22 Feb 1880 at his son’s residence, Carbondale (Leaton)
Abram Walker and Rhoda Beauchamp (lead; Levi Walker, about 1905)
Deacon 9 Oct 1831 (Bp Roberts); elder 3 Oct 1833 (Bp Soule)

xu3-002.note: Named only in the 1921 Southern Illinois Conference memoir of her son, which calls him the son of Simeon and Elizabeth Sharpe Walker. No dates or places are known. That she was the wife of the Rev. Simeon Walker of Leaton’s history, and not only of a man of the same name, rests on the memoir’s statement that Levi’s father was an itinerant Methodist preacher and on the match of Levi’s birth year and county with Simeon’s itinerant years.
kv: Memoir of Levi Sharpe Walker, 1921 conference minutes

MAT_JAMES_WILLIS_STACY.note: A Stacy family history lists Emory Ann Stacy Turner (1871–1964) among his and Mary Jane Edwards's children, and its 1880 census transcription, Madison County, Texas, has a daughter Emerva A., 9. The unusual given name matches “Emory A. Stacy” on Beulah Phillips's Social Security application,. Emma’s 1964 Texas death certificate names James Stacey and Mary Edwards as her parents, which proves the link.

MAT_ALEXANDER_FRANKLIN_STACY.note: Father of James Willis Stacy: the 1850 census of Natchitoches Parish, as transcribed in the Stacy family history, lists “Jas W 3” in the household of A. F. MAT_CLEMENT_LOGAN.note: In the 1850 census of Greene County, Alabama, dwelling 1131, Clement Logan, 33, a farmer born in South Carolina, heads a household with Mary A., 28, Elizabeth H., 8, Dudley, 3, and Martha, 6 months. Dudley Logan's memorial says he came from Greene County and names his father James Clement Logan. Leroy and Willis Logan, also South Carolina born, lived next door. He married Mary A. Williams in Greene County on 18 April 1839, and the 1850 slave schedule lists eight people enslaved by him. By 1860 Dudley, 14, and Martha, 9, were living with the Pool family. His will, dated 17 April 1854, was proved on 9 October 1854, when a guardian ad litem was named for Elizabeth Logan, Dudley T. Logan and Martha Logan, his minor heirs and only surviving children (Greene County Will Records C-D, pp. 369-370). His estate file names the same three heirs; Noah Harris was executor until the final settlement of 1866-68. He was named executor and residuary legatee in his mother Martha Logan's will of 1852. Witnesses to his will were Willis Logan, Alvis L. Logan and John C. McIntyre.

MAT_MARY_A_LOGAN.note: Clement Logan's wife in the 1850 Greene County household that includes Dudley, 3. A Clemmons Logan married Mary A. Williams in Greene County on 18 April 1839, which fits the 1850 wife, Mary A., 28. Dudley's memorial names his mother Martha Calhoun instead, so she stays probable, not proven. Not named in her husband's will of April 1854 or at its probate, where Elizabeth, Dudley and Martha are called his only surviving children; she had probably died by then. Her identity as Dudley's mother remains probable (the 1839 marriage and 1850 household).

MAT_CALVIN_MERRY.note: Lewis Merry's father. Lewis named his parents as Calvin and Elizabeth Merry on Choctaw Dawes card 5754, and the 1880 census of Monroe Township, Sevier County, Arkansas (indexed under “Tracy”) lists Calvin, 48, a farmer born in Arkansas, with Eliza J., 43, and sons Festus Lee, Benjamin F., Joshua L. (8), John H. and George G. He married Eliza McGregor at Mount Ida, Montgomery County, on 18 November 1859. A later marriage (1888) and a death about 1896 at Goodland are leads only. A Calvin Merry sat on the first grand jury of Hempstead County, Arkansas, on 28 June 1819; nothing yet connects that man, who was grown by 1790, to this Calvin, born about 1832, though he could have been a grandfather.

MAT_ELIZA_JANE_MCGREGOR_MERRY.note: Lewis Merry's mother: “Elizabeth” on his Dawes card, Eliza J., 43, in the 1880 Sevier County household, and “Eliza McGreggory” on her son Benjamin Franklin Merry's 1959 Texas death certificate. Married Calvin Merry at Mount Ida, Arkansas, on 18 November 1859. She probably died before 1888.

xr7-001.note: His will, proved in Chester District in November 1844 (Book A1 p. 32, Apt. 89, Pkg. 1417), leaves property to 'my son Vincent Brown Tims' and to his wife Winifred. Known from a family transcription (Lucille Brown, via the Carolina Magic blog, 2013); the original has not been read. Winifred is not shown to be Vincent's mother, so no mother is entered. Very probably the son Joseph named in the earlier Chester will of Joseph Tims (d. 16 Aug 1801) and Mary Glover, whose daughter Sarah Estes the same will names (Seltzer 1981; Tims Bible). Winifred, his widow, remains unconfirmed as Vincent's mother. The original 1841 will names sons Vincent Brown, Alford, John and Joseph T. and daughters Harriet Farrar, Elizabeth Wages(?) and Sarah Castles(?). A Joseph who was the son of Joseph (d. 1801) and Mary is proven living in Chester in 1827; that he is this testator is probable. Winifred was probably a later wife (about 39 in 1850), not Vincent's mother.

Father of Sarah Tims Estes (1776-1849; Seltzer, Cary-Estes Genealogy, 1981) and of Amos Tims (1771-1867). The Chester will the family calls his first names sons Amos, John and Joseph and daughters Sarah Estes, Mary Carter, Frances Boyd and Elizabeth Tims.
